vlog.Problematic:
In the previous AeroData post, I proposed a second-generation transmitter: STM32 Nucleo-F411RE, BMI270 IMU, IIS2MDC magnetometer, BMP581 barometer, MAX-M10S GNSS, and an SX1262 LoRa radio. Those parts were chosen against accuracy, lifecycle, compliance, and power requirements.

The problem is that these components are not available in Tunisia. I cannot buy them locally, so I cannot build the board, and the design stays untested on paper.

I still needed to know whether the chosen sensor suite, estimation algorithms, and RF link would work together before committing to hardware.
vlog.Features:
AeroData Sim is a Python UAV navigation and telemetry simulation. It covers the full chain from true motion to ground-received data.

It starts by generating a synthetic aircraft trajectory in the NED frame, which serves as ground truth. From that trajectory, it produces noisy, biased measurements from the BMI270 (IMU), IIS2MDC (magnetometer), BMP581 (barometer), and MAX-M10S (GNSS).

Onboard estimation runs a quaternion-based Multiplicative Extended Kalman Filter (MEKF) for 3D attitude and gyro bias, plus a three-state Kalman filter for altitude, vertical velocity, and barometer bias.

The estimated telemetry is packed into binary frames with sync words, message IDs, timestamps, and CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE checksums. These frames pass through a simulated SX1262 LoRa link with configurable airtime, packet loss, propagation delay, and link statistics.

Everything is logged to CSV, and Matplotlib diagnostics compare true states, raw measurements, complementary-filter baselines, and filter estimates. The code is modular and covered by 21 automated tests.
vlog.Challenges:
Navigation conventions were the first difficulty. Frame definitions (NED, body), quaternion conventions, and sign handling are easy to get subtly wrong, and errors can hide behind plausible-looking plots.

Estimator correctness was the second. The MEKF’s attitude error state and gyro bias estimation had to be validated against known truth, not just inspected visually.

The barometer offset was the most concrete bug. The altitude filter initially showed a persistent offset. Tracing it and adding barometer bias as a filter state fixed it, and altitude tracking was then validated against the true trajectory.

Finally, protocol integrity mattered. Binary framing and CRC checks had to hold up under packet loss and delay, which is why the link model and the tests were built together.
vlog.Solution:
Since the hardware is out of reach, I built the system in simulation. The simulator makes the second-generation design testable now: the same sensors, the same estimation problem, and the same radio, with ground truth available for every state.

It was also a deliberate opportunity to improve my Python. The project pushed me on modular package structure, numerical code with NumPy, binary data handling, test-driven development, and plotting for diagnostics.
vlog.LearningOutcomes: I implemented a quaternion MEKF and a bias-augmented altitude Kalman filter from scratch, and modeled realistic sensor noise and bias from datasheet-level behavior. I designed and validated a binary telemetry protocol with CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE, and modeled a LoRa link including airtime, loss, and delay. Throughout, I wrote modular, tested Python (21 tests) with structured diagnostics.
vlog.WhatToDoDifferently: I would validate each estimator against ground truth in isolation before integrating the full chain. I would also fix navigation and quaternion conventions in one documented place at the start, and write the tests alongside each module instead of after.
vlog.FutureWork:
#### Hardware side

Source the second-generation components and build the real system: STM32 Nucleo-F411RE, BMI270, IIS2MDC, BMP581, MAX-M10S, and SX1262 (E22-900M22S). Then log real flight or bench data and compare it with the simulation outputs. This closes the loop: if simulated noise models, estimation error, and link behavior match measured behavior, the simulator is validated. Where they don’t, the models get corrected.

#### Software side

The current simulator proves the estimation code works for one fixed configuration with all sensors healthy. The next step is a user-configurable sensor-fusion and telemetry qualification platform.

Engineers would select a sensor suite from a library instead of a hard-coded one, then inject timed or probabilistic faults such as GPS outage, barometer freeze, and magnetometer interference. The full RF chain, with binary framing and LoRa transmission including packet loss and delay, would let errors be measured both onboard and as received on the ground.

Runs would be organized as a 3D batch matrix of sensor configuration × fault profile × RF quality, executed automatically. The outputs would be ranked comparisons: end-to-end RMSE (onboard vs. ground-received), packet-loss statistics, and cost-vs-accuracy Pareto frontiers.

This changes the question the tool answers. Instead of “does my Kalman filter work?”, it answers “which sensor set, under which failure conditions, over which radio link, meets a mission requirement at the lowest cost?” That makes it useful for procurement, regulatory, and design decisions, and turns a working algorithm into a systems-engineering qualification tool.
